newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec separatists slip; Liberals lead nationally.
newsitem.headline: Quebec separatists slip; Liberals lead nationally.

text.p: The separatist Bloc Quebecois party is losing voter support in Canada's Quebec province, where the ruling Liberals and the Progressive Conservative Party have surged, an opinion poll showed on Saturday.

A separate poll showed the Liberals continuing to hold a wide lead across the country ahead of Canada's June 2 federal election, but the lead was not quite as wide as other recent surveys have indicated.

The national poll, conducted for the CTV television network and the Southam newspaper chain, found that the Liberals had the support of 42 percent of voters who had made up their minds. Other surveys in recent weeks had given them leads of 44 percent to 47.6 percent.

Political analysts warned against giving too much weight to any single poll result and noted that the margins of error in the polls -- 1.9 to 3.2 percentage points -- made it difficult to interpret the difference as a clear sign of erosion in Liberal support.

The CTV/Southam poll found the Progressive Conservatives had 19 percent support, the right-wing Reform party 18 percent, the left-wing New Democratic Party 11 percent and the Bloc Quebecois 9 percent, with 8 percent of voters undecided.
For the survey, the Angus Reid organisation questioned 3,208 Canadians from May 5 to 8. The results are considered accurate within 2.25 percentage points.

In the closely watched Quebec race, a poll released on Saturday found that for the first time since the last election, in 1993, more Quebec voters who had decided which party to support said they intended to vote for the Liberals than for the Bloc Quebecois.
Groupe Leger & Leger took the poll for the Globe and Mail and Le Journal de Montreal newspapers over four days last week, starting on Tuesday.

It found that 38.8 percent of Quebec voters who had decided on a party said they intended to vote for the Liberals, up from 36.9 percent in a poll two weeks earlier. The number intending to back the Bloc Quebecois fell to 37.1 percent from 43.1 percent.

Much of the drop reflected a gain for the Conservatives. A total of 19.8 percent of voters who had decided said they preferred the Conservatives, a rise from 14.6 percent. Overall, 20.4 percent of those questioned described themselves as undecided.
The poll covered 1,008 voters and had a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points 19 times out of 20.

Quebec's independence drive turned into a major issue late this week, the second week of the election campaign, as the Liberals under Prime Minister Jean Chretien accused the separatists of deceiving Quebeckers about their plans.

Chretien, who is from Quebec, has fought efforts by the Bloc Quebecois to take the province out of Canada. The federalist camp narrowly lost a referendum on the question in 1995, and another referendum is widely expected within the next few years.

A Quebec newspaper reported this week that former Quebec Premier Jacques Parizeau had planned to declare unilateral independence immediately if the separatists won the 1995 referendum. Publicly, he had promised to move slowly and negotiate an arrangement maintaining many links with Canada.

Parizeau denied the report, but not before it caused confusion in the separatist camp and provoked harsh rhetoric from the Liberals and other unity supporters. The controversy was not the first stumble for the Bloc Quebecois' election campaign, which political analysts have called poorly handled.

Despite the erosion in support, the Bloc Quebecois still appears likely to win at least 40 parliamentary seats, pollster Jean-Marc Leger told the Globe. He said the results of the poll had been consistent over four days of polling, suggesting that the controversy over Parizeau's plans had had little immediate impact.
